clinical_category: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control

semantic_correction.stem: At the end of a hemodialysis treatment, a nurse removes contaminated fistula needles. Which action best follows OSHA bloodborne-pathogen and sharps-safety requirements?

options.A: Activate the needle's safety feature when present and discard it promptly into the appropriate sharps container without routine recapping.
options.B: Recap the contaminated needle with two hands before carrying it to the sharps container.
options.C: Place used needles on the work surface until station cleanup is complete, then discard them together.
options.D: Bend or break the contaminated needle before disposal so it takes less space in the sharps container.

semantic_correction.rationale: OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens Standard requires engineering and work-practice controls to minimize occupational exposure to blood and contaminated sharps. Current OSHA guidance recommends using sharps with engineered injury protection, activating safety features, avoiding routine recapping, shearing, or breaking of contaminated needles, and disposing of contaminated sharps immediately or as soon as feasible in an appropriate puncture-resistant sharps container. OSHA permits recapping or needle removal only in limited circumstances when no alternative is feasible or a specific procedure requires it, using a mechanical device or one-handed technique. None of those exceptions applies in this post-use disposal scenario, so option A is correct.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Prevent occupational bloodborne-pathogen exposure by activating available sharps-safety features and promptly disposing of contaminated dialysis needles without routine recapping, bending, or breaking.
semantic_correction.source_document_title: Bloodborne Pathogens — General Guidance; 29 CFR 1910.1030 Bloodborne Pathogens
semantic_correction.source_version_date: Current OSHA guidance and regulation accessed August 21, 2026
semantic_correction.source_locator: OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens General Guidance — use SESIPs, always activate safety features, do not recap/shear/break contaminated needles, immediately dispose in secured puncture-resistant sharps containers. 29 CFR 1910.1030(d)(2)(vii) — contaminated needles shall not be bent, recapped, or removed except limited specified circumstances; shearing/breaking prohibited. 1910.1030(d)(4)(iii)(A)(1) — contaminated sharps discarded immediately or as soon as feasible in appropriate containers
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: After use, contaminated needles should be handled with engineering/work-practice controls, available safety features activated, and sharps discarded promptly into appropriate containers without routine two-handed recapping, bending, shearing, or breaking.

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup: shortened the uniquely long correct answer, retained OSHA's limited recapping exception in the rationale rather than falsely treating the prohibition as exceptionless, and rebuilt distractors around actual unsafe post-use sharps practices.

audit_findings_append.finding: The original answer was uniquely longest. The revised item tests prompt disposal and safety-feature use while accurately preserving OSHA's narrow recapping exceptions.

option_audit.A: Correct. It matches OSHA engineering-control, safety-feature, and prompt sharps-disposal guidance for routine post-use handling.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. Routine two-handed recapping is not permitted; limited exceptions require a mechanical device or one-handed technique.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. Leaving contaminated sharps on a work surface delays disposal and increases exposure risk.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. Shearing or breaking contaminated needles is prohibited, and bending is not permitted in routine disposal.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A is the only option consistent with routine post-use OSHA sharps controls; the regulation's narrow recapping exception is not triggered by the scenario.
cueing_check: All four choices are immediate post-use sharps actions of comparable length and specificity; no absolute-word or unique-length cue identifies A.
